exchanges.interviewer: Hi, thanks for taking the time. To start, could you tell me about your role as an accounts payable clerk — what you're mainly responsible for, and who you work with most?
exchanges.reply: I'm mainly responsible for processing the supplier and subcontractor invoices that come into Kaarna, which is about 70 a day, and getting them entered and approved so they can be paid on time. Day to day I work most closely with the department heads, since anything over 2,000 euros needs their approval before I can release it. I also deal with our subcontractors when there's a question about an invoice.

exchanges.interviewer: 70 invoices a day is a solid volume. Besides entering and routing invoices for approval, are there other things you're responsible for — like handling payment runs, resolving supplier queries, or reconciling accounts?
exchanges.reply: Mostly the entering, routing and chasing approvals is what fills my day, and I don't run the payment batches myself, so I'm not the one doing the bank side of things. Supplier questions do come my way when an invoice doesn't match what we expected, and I sort those out with the supplier directly. I wouldn't say I do account reconciliation; that sits with someone else in the finance team.

exchanges.interviewer: That's helpful context. Who sits in the finance team with you, and who else do you regularly hand off to or get invoices from — like a procurement team, or is it mostly direct from suppliers?
exchanges.reply: Most of the invoices come straight from suppliers and subcontractors to our invoices@ mailbox, about 80 percent of them as PDF attachments, and the rest arrive as e-invoices that flow in automatically. I don't think we have a separate procurement team handling them first; the department heads are the ones who approve anything over 2,000 euros. I'm not certain of the full make-up of the finance team beyond the people I work with directly, so I'd check that with someone in management.

exchanges.interviewer: That gives me a good picture, thanks. Let's walk through a typical day — could you tell me what you did yesterday, from when you started working?
exchanges.reply: I started by going through the invoices@ mailbox, and yesterday there were around 70 invoices waiting, most of them PDFs that I had to open and type into Procountor one by one. For each one I enter the supplier, invoice number, due date, net amount, VAT and cost centre, which takes me about 3 minutes, so that alone is roughly 3 hours of my morning. Anything over 2,000 euros I then send to the department head by email and wait on, and that's where a fair bit of my afternoon goes.

exchanges.interviewer: I noticed you mentioned Procountor this time, rather than Kaarna — are those two different systems you use together, or is Kaarna another name for the same one?
exchanges.reply: Kaarna is the name of the company, and Procountor is the accounting system I type the invoices into, so they're two different things. I'm not sure about the technical setup behind it, like whether it's connected to anything else, so that's a question for IT or whoever manages the finance tools.

exchanges.interviewer: Good, that clears it up. Beyond the morning entry and afternoon approval-chasing, what does the rest of your day or week typically look like — any other recurring tasks?
exchanges.reply: The main other recurring task is chasing approvals, which I do by phone every Thursday, because invoices over 2,000 euros usually take 3 to 6 working days to come back from the department head. Late approvals can mean we lose early-payment discounts and sometimes pay late fees. Beyond that, the rest of the week is mostly more of the same invoice entry, and I also deal with typing mistakes when they come up, since swapped digits in amounts or reference numbers lead to about 5 payment corrections a month.

exchanges.interviewer: That 3-6 day approval wait with real cost impact is a key detail. Walk me through one recent case where an approval was late and it caused a late fee or lost discount — what happened, step by step?
exchanges.reply: I don't have a specific recent case I can walk you through step by step, and I'd rather not make one up. What I can tell you is the usual pattern: I email the PDF to the department head, the approval often takes 3 to 6 working days, and if it hasn't come back by the Thursday I phone to chase it. When it runs past the early-payment date, we lose the discount, and occasionally the invoice ends up paid late and a late fee is charged. If you want an actual example with dates and amounts, the payment records in Procountor or whoever handles the payment runs would have the details.

exchanges.interviewer: That's fair, thanks for the honest answer. On the typing mistakes — walk me through one recent case: how did the error get caught, what did you have to do to fix it, and how long did that take?
exchanges.reply: I don't have a specific recent case I can take you through step by step, so I won't invent one. What I can say is that the mistakes are usually swapped digits in an amount or a reference number, which I type in by hand from the PDF, and they come to about five payment corrections a month. The usual fix is correcting the entry in Procountor and making sure the payment is sorted out with the supplier, but for the exact timing and steps on a real case, the payment records or whoever handles the payment runs would have the detail.

exchanges.interviewer: No specific example available this time — that's fine. When you catch a typing mistake yourself, before it becomes a payment correction, what usually tips you off that something's wrong?
exchanges.reply: Usually it's a mismatch when I check the entry against the PDF, or a number that looks off compared with what I'd expect from that supplier. Swapped digits are the usual culprit, so I'll sometimes notice a reference number that doesn't match the invoice in front of me. I don't have a particular routine beyond that, so it's mostly down to care and a second look before I save the entry.

exchanges.interviewer: So some mistakes slip through if that "second look" doesn't catch them. When one does slip through and gets paid, how do you typically find out — does the supplier call you, or does it show up some other way?
exchanges.reply: I don't have a detailed picture of how each one surfaces, so I'd rather not guess at the exact route. What I can say is that the payment corrections I deal with come to about five a month, and they're usually caught after the payment has gone out. For the specifics of how a given one was flagged, the payment records or whoever handles the payment runs would be the right people to ask.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a fair boundary — I'll leave those details with the payment team. When you do find out about a slipped-through mistake, what's your part in fixing it — do you correct the Procountor entry, contact the supplier, or something else?
exchanges.reply: Yes, my part is usually correcting the entry in Procountor so the record matches the actual invoice, and then I deal with the supplier about the wrong amount or reference so the right money or reference gets sorted out. I'm not the one doing the payment itself, so any correction to the money going out would go through the payment side. For the exact steps on a particular correction, the payment team would be the better source.

exchanges.interviewer: That gives me a clear picture of your part in the fix. One more on flows — once you correct an entry in Procountor, does anyone downstream need to know about that change, or does it just update automatically for the payment team to see?
exchanges.reply: I'm not certain how the change is picked up downstream, because I don't see the payment side of Procountor and I don't know whether it updates automatically or needs a message to anyone. From my end, I save the corrected entry and then deal with the supplier, but I don't routinely send anyone a note about it. The payment team or whoever manages the Procountor setup would know how their side is notified.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a useful gap to flag. Shifting focus slightly — when you route an invoice over 2,000 euros to a department head by email, how do you know the approval has actually come back: a reply email, a stamp, something in Procountor?
exchanges.reply: I usually know it's back when the department head replies to my email with the PDF marked as approved, and I then record the approval in Procountor before the payment is released. If I haven't heard by the Thursday, I phone them to ask, which is why I end up chasing so many of these by phone. I'm not sure whether Procountor has its own approval step or stamp that I'd use, since I've only ever worked from the email reply.

exchanges.interviewer: Thinking about a typical approved invoice — once the department head emails back the marked-up PDF, what do you actually do with that email: do you file it, attach it in Procountor, or just use it as a trigger to update the status?
exchanges.reply: I save the marked-up PDF from the reply and attach it to the invoice record in Procountor, so the approval sits alongside the invoice itself. Then I update the status so it's ready for payment. I'm not sure whether the email itself is kept anywhere else, so I'd check with the finance team about their filing rules.

exchanges.interviewer: That clarifies the manual attach-and-update step well. Last question: is there anything important about your work that I haven't asked about?
Hi, thanks for taking the time. To start, could you tell me a bit about your role as financial controller and who you mainly work with day to day?
exchanges.reply: Thanks for having me. I'm the financial controller here at Kaarna, so I run the month-end close, prepare the monthly management report for the leadership team, and keep an eye on how the numbers hang together across the company. Day to day I work most closely with the accounts payable and billing people, and with dispatch and customer service, because a lot of what ends up in my numbers starts with their work. The company has grown from a much smaller operation to about 140 people and 45 trucks, and honestly my reporting processes have had to keep up with that, which is something we can get into later.

exchanges.interviewer: That growth context is helpful. Beyond the month-end close and management report, what other responsibilities fall under your role — things like budgeting, audit, cash flow, or compliance?
exchanges.reply: Beyond the close and the management report, the other piece on my desk is purchase approvals. Requests come to me and I usually get back to people within a day, so that part isn't a bottleneck. I also do a lot of the reconciliation work behind the close, which takes a good chunk of the first week of

exchanges.interviewer: Got cut off there — you mentioned reconciliation takes a chunk of the first week. Could you finish that thought, what does that reconciliation work involve?
exchanges.reply: Sorry about that, I got carried away. The main reconciliation is matching subcontractor freight invoices against our delivery records. The first four working days of every month go to that, because the invoices were typed into Procountor separately from the TMS, so I export both to Excel and match them by hand. It's tedious, but it's also the part where I catch the mismatches, and once the matching is done the close itself moves quickly.

exchanges.interviewer: That matching process sounds like a real pain point already. You mentioned earlier that reporting has had to scale with the company's growth to 140 people and 45 trucks — what specifically broke or got harder as that happened?
exchanges.reply: The clearest example is that the same information gets typed in more than once. A delivery gets confirmed in the TMS, then dispatch re-types the confirmation into the billing spreadsheet, and the subcontractor invoice gets keyed separately into Procountor, so the same data lives in email, the TMS, billing and Procountor. Because nothing links these systems directly, I end up matching by hand, and the billing side runs at roughly 2 percent of deliveries billed wrong or late. I'd say the reporting itself has held up fine, since producing the monthly management report in Excel and PowerPoint takes about a day and I don't mind that. The real strain is upstream, in the manual handoffs that were tolerable when we had a fraction of today's volume.

exchanges.interviewer: That 2% billing error rate is a concrete number worth digging into. Can you walk me through a recent case where a delivery got billed wrong or late — where in that chain did it break down?
exchanges.reply: I don't have a specific recent case to walk you through, and I'd rather not invent one. What I can tell you is where the chain is weakest based on how it's built. A delivery is confirmed in the TMS, then dispatch re-types that confirmation into the billing spreadsheet, so the most likely point of failure is that re-keying step: a wrong quantity, a wrong date, or a delivery that was confirmed late and never made it across. The 2 percent figure is the rough share of deliveries that end up billed wrong or late from that process overall. If you want an actual example, the billing or dispatch team would be better placed to pull one from their records, because they see the individual mistakes and I only see the effect on the close.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a fair distinction, thanks for being clear about where your visibility ends. From your side, then, how do you actually discover that something was billed wrong or late — is it something you catch during the matching, or does it surface later, like a customer complaint?
exchanges.reply: Mostly I catch it during the matching, though it isn't always clean. When I reconcile subcontractor invoices against delivery records in the first four working days, I'm looking at the cost side, so a mismatch shows up as a freight cost that doesn't line up with a confirmed delivery, or a delivery with no matching invoice. On the billing side I see it less directly, because customer invoices are built from the billing spreadsheet, and I don't re-check each line against the TMS the way I do with subcontractor invoices. So a wrong or late customer bill tends to show up when someone notices the revenue for a period looks off, or when the customer raises it, and I'd have to ask the billing team how those cases typically come to light. That gap is one I'd want to understand better before saying anything firm about it.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a useful gap to flag. When a mismatch does turn up during your subcontractor reconciliation — a freight cost with no matching delivery, say — what do you actually do to resolve it, and roughly how long does that take per case?
exchanges.reply: When a mismatch turns up, the first thing I do is check whether the delivery exists in the TMS at all, because sometimes the invoice refers to a load that was confirmed under a different reference or date. If the delivery is there but the invoice doesn't match on price or quantity, I go back to the subcontractor's invoice and the rate agreed for that route, and that usually settles it within a few minutes. If there's no delivery record at all, I contact dispatch to ask whether the load ran, and that's where it can drag, because they're busy and it sometimes takes a day or two to get a clear answer. On average I'd say most cases take a few minutes to resolve on my side, and the occasional one with no clear answer from dispatch can hold up the close for a couple of days. I don't keep a log of these, so those numbers are my rough sense rather than measured figures.

exchanges.interviewer: That dispatch delay is a good concrete bottleneck — thanks for the detail. Now, on that re-typing you mentioned: delivery confirmed in TMS, then retyped into the billing spreadsheet, and the subcontractor invoice keyed into Procountor — can you walk me through that chain step by step, including who does each step and roughly how long each takes?
exchanges.reply: Here's how I understand the chain, though I should be clear I don't do the re-typing myself, so the timings are my rough sense rather than measured figures. Step one is the delivery getting confirmed in the TMS, which is done by dispatch once the load is complete. Step two is dispatch re-typing that confirmation into the billing spreadsheet, which the billing team then uses to raise customer invoices, and I'd guess that happens within a day or two of delivery, though billing would know the real turnaround. Step three is the subcontractor invoice arriving by email and being keyed into Procountor, which I believe is handled by accounts payable, and that's where the duplication sits, because the same delivery now exists in the TMS, the billing sheet and Procountor. I don't know exactly how long each keying step takes per delivery, so for the actual minutes per entry I'd ask dispatch and AP directly.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a clear picture of the chain. How does the subcontractor invoice actually arrive — is it a PDF by email that AP then manually types into Procountor line by line, or does it come in some other form?
exchanges.reply: From what I understand, subcontractor invoices arrive by email, usually as PDFs, and AP then keys them into Procountor line by line. I don't handle that keying myself, so I can't tell you the exact format each subcontractor uses or whether any of them send structured files. What I do see is the result: the invoices reach me in Procountor already typed, and that's the version I export to Excel to match against the TMS. If you want the details of the intake itself, the AP team is the right people to ask.

exchanges.interviewer: Makes sense, that's a natural line for AP to answer. Once Procountor has the subcontractor invoice and you've exported both that and the TMS data to Excel for matching, what does that matching actually look like — are you using formulas, pivot tables, manual line-by-line eyeballing?
exchanges.reply: It's a mix, and I'd say it leans more on my own spreadsheet work than on eyeballing every line. I export the Procountor invoice lines and the TMS delivery records, then use lookup formulas to pair them on shared fields like the load reference, date and route, and pivot tables to total freight cost per subcontractor and per period so I can see the overall picture. Anything that doesn't pair cleanly, roughly one invoice in ten by my rough sense, gets pulled into a separate tab and I go through those by hand, which is where the dispatch questions come from. The formulas handle the bulk well, but they only work as cleanly as the reference numbers were typed consistently in the first place, so a slightly different reference format between the two systems is what usually forces the manual step. I don't track the exact share anywhere, so treat that one-in-ten as an estimate.

exchanges.interviewer: That one-in-ten mismatch rate from inconsistent reference formats is a good concrete detail. When you build those lookup formulas and pivot tables each month, do you rebuild them from scratch on the new export, or do you have a template file you reuse and just refresh the data in?
exchanges.reply: I reuse a template. The workbook I keep has the lookup formulas already set up on the matching tab and the pivot tables pointing at the summary range, so each month I paste the new Procountor and TMS exports into the input sheets and refresh the pivots. The only real adjustment is when the export layout shifts, for example if a column moves or a new subcontractor appears, and then I fix the ranges by hand. So that's the option that fits: template reuse with a refresh, not a rebuild from scratch. It's been stable enough that I haven't felt the need to rebuild it, although it does depend on me keeping that one file up to date.

exchanges.interviewer: That's helpful, thanks. Shifting to the billing side for a moment — when a customer invoice turns out wrong or late, how does the billing team typically find out, and what do they do to fix it?
exchanges.reply: I can't speak for how the billing team handles this in detail, since that sits outside my desk. From my side, the cases I'd expect to reach me are the ones that show up as revenue looking off for a period, or where a customer has raised it, and I'd have to ask billing how they usually learn about an error and what they do to correct it. I'd rather point you to them than guess at their process, because they're the ones who see the individual invoices and corrections. If it helps, I can tell you what the revenue side of a correction looks like in the close, but the step-by-step fix belongs to billing.

exchanges.interviewer: That's fair, I'll follow up with billing directly on that. Sticking with handoffs on your side — once your month-end reconciliation and matching is done, who's waiting on your output, and how does it get to them?
exchanges.reply: Once the matching is done and the close is locked, the main people waiting on my output are the leadership team, who get the monthly management report, and whoever needs the final cost and revenue figures for the period. The management report is an Excel workbook with a PowerPoint built from it, which I produce over about a day and send out by email. I also share the reconciled subcontractor cost summary with dispatch and AP when there are open items, because those are the people who can clear the mismatches, so that goes back the same way, by email with the workbook attached. Honestly it's a fairly simple handoff, and I don't see it as the problem; the friction is still in getting the underlying data right before I get to it.

exchanges.interviewer: That gives a complete picture of the downstream side. Does leadership or anyone else ever wait on that report past your usual one-day turnaround, or does it reliably go out on schedule?
exchanges.reply: It goes out on schedule as far as I know. The report takes me about a day to produce once the close is locked, and since the close itself usually finishes after the first four working days, the report generally lands within the first week of the month. I can't recall anyone chasing me for it, but I don't keep a record of when it's been delivered, so I can't give you a count of late cases. The real timing risk is upstream: if a mismatch with dispatch drags on for a couple of days, the close slips and the report slips with it.

exchanges.interviewer: That connects the upstream bottleneck to the final deadline clearly, thanks. One last question: is there anything important about your work that I haven't asked about?
exchanges.reply: Yes, one thing I'd want on the record is the approvals side, because I think I've been too quick to wave it off. I do answer purchase requests within a day, and that part works well for me, but the approvals only move as fast as the information attached to each request, and that's often thin. I'd also say the piece that bothers me most isn't any single step but the fact that the same delivery data gets keyed two or three times across email, the TMS, billing and Procountor. Each copy is a chance for a mismatch, and that's what drives the matching work that eats my first four days. The company grew faster than the systems connecting them, and I'd rather someone looked at that chain end to end than at any one desk in isolation.

exchanges.interviewer:
Thank you, that's a really useful note to end on, especially the point about the same delivery being keyed multiple times across systems.

Here's my summary: you're the controller running month-end close and the management report, with purchase approvals and reconciliation as recurring work. The core pain is upstream: delivery data gets retyped across TMS, billing spreadsheet and Procountor, causing ~1-in-10 reference mismatches you resolve by hand using a reused Excel template. Dispatch follow-ups on missing delivery records can stall close by 1-2 days. Downstream, your report reliably goes out within a week, no issues there. Billing-side invoice errors are outside your visibility - flagged for follow-up. Purchase approvals are fast but limited by thin request detail.

To start, could you tell me what you're responsible for as evening/night shift supervisor, and who you mainly work with during a shift?
exchanges.reply: I run the evening and night shifts at the cross-dock terminal, so it's 14:00 to 22:00 or 22:00 to 06:00, depending on the rota. I have 12 warehouse workers on my shift, and they're the people I work with most. Day to day that means keeping the floor moving, making sure trucks are loaded and out on time, and dealing with whatever breaks down or goes missing during the shift.

exchanges.interviewer: Besides your 12 warehouse workers, do you coordinate with other roles too, like dispatch, drivers, or the day shift supervisor?
exchanges.reply: The main link

exchanges.interviewer: Could you say more about that - who's the main link, and what do you coordinate with them on?
exchanges.reply: The main link is the next shift. At the end of every shift I fill in a paper A4 handover form covering open shipments, damaged goods, forklift faults and missing staff, and leave it on the desk in the terminal office. About once a week it gets lost, coffee-stained or becomes unreadable, and then the next shift has to walk the floor and recheck everything, which takes 20 to 30 minutes.

exchanges.interviewer: That handover form issue is useful to know. Let's talk about a typical shift now - walking me through yesterday, or a recent typical shift, from start to finish?
exchanges.reply: Let me walk you through a recent evening shift, from 14:00. I start by checking the handover from the day shift, which is the same paper form I described, and see what's open. Then I split the 12 workers across loading bays and check the dock schedule, making sure trucks are ready for the outbound runs. Through the shift I'm dealing with whatever comes up, like a damaged pallet or a forklift that won't start, and at 22:00 I fill in the A4 handover form for the night shift and leave it on the office desk.

exchanges.interviewer: Of those activities - checking handover, splitting workers across bays, tracking the dock schedule, handling breakdowns, end-of-shift paperwork - roughly how do the hours split across an 8-hour shift?
exchanges.reply: I don't have exact timings logged, so I can't give you precise figures, but from memory the handover check at the start takes maybe 20 to 30 minutes, and the end-of-shift form another 15 to 20. Most of the rest goes on the floor: positioning people across the bays, watching the dock schedule, and dealing with breakdowns, which can eat up an hour on a bad night. If you need real numbers, the rota and the terminal logs would be better than my guesses.

exchanges.interviewer: That gives a good picture. On a night with a breakdown eating up an hour, what usually causes it — is it more often equipment failure, damaged goods, or something else?
exchanges.reply: Equipment failure is the one that most often eats up the hour, and the forklifts are the main culprit. The problem is often not the breakdown itself but getting the part: spare parts over 500 euros need the terminal manager's approval by email, and that approval can sit in an inbox so a broken forklift waits three or four days for the part. So on those nights I'm not just fixing something, I'm working around a machine that's out of action for days.

exchanges.interviewer: That forklift approval delay is a good example of a bottleneck to flag later. Going back to the handover form itself - what exactly do you write on it by hand, and does anyone re-type or re-enter that information anywhere else afterward?
exchanges.reply: I write down the open shipments, any damaged goods, forklift faults, and missing staff, all by hand on the A4 sheet. As far as I know nobody re-types it anywhere; it stays on the desk in the terminal office and the next shift works from that paper. If it goes missing or gets coffee on it, that's when the walk-the-floor recheck happens, but I'm not aware of it being entered into a system afterwards.

exchanges.interviewer: Good to know that the form stays purely on paper. Besides the handover form, are there other things during a shift you record by hand - like damage reports, missing stock, or incident notes - before they end up anywhere else?
exchanges.reply: Mostly it's the same A4 handover form, since damaged goods, forklift faults and missing staff all go on it. I don't keep a separate damage report or incident book myself, so I can't say what happens to those beyond the form. For anything more specific, like how a missing-stock case gets logged in the system, the customer service desk or the terminal manager would know better than I do.

exchanges.interviewer: Thinking about a specific case - when a missing stock item turns up during your shift, what do you actually do in that moment, step by step, before it gets written on the handover form?
exchanges.reply: When a missing item turns up, I first go and physically check it: find the pallet or bay, confirm the consignment note matches what's there, and make sure it's not just sitting in the wrong place. Then I get one of the lads to move it to the right bay or outbound door so it doesn't hold anything up. Only after that do I put it on the handover form, with the shipment reference and where it is now, so the next shift knows it's sorted. I don't have a fixed checklist beyond that, so the detail depends on the case.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a clear walkthrough. When you confirm the consignment note against what's physically there, do you check it against a paper document, or something on a screen or handheld scanner?
exchanges.reply: Mostly it's the paper consignment note that comes with the pallet, so I compare the reference and the item count with what's on the pallet itself. I don't use a handheld scanner for that check on my shift. If the note and the load don't match, I'd write it up on the handover form and let the day side or the customer service desk sort out the system side.

exchanges.interviewer: That confirms the consignment check is paper-based end to end. Going back to the lost or coffee-stained handover form - when that happens about once a week, what does the recheck actually involve, and who does it?
exchanges.reply: The next shift does the recheck, so whoever is on the incoming evening or night shift, usually me or the shift lead on the other rota. They walk the whole floor and go bay by bay, checking open shipments, damaged goods, forklift faults and missing staff against what's physically there, since they have no reliable paper to go on. It takes 20 to 30 minutes each time, which is time the shift could otherwise spend on the trucks.

exchanges.interviewer: Besides the handover form going missing, what's another problem that comes up regularly - things like errors, rework, or missing information that trip up the shift?
exchanges.reply: Honestly, the one that comes up most regularly after the handover form is the forklift part approval. A broken forklift can sit for three or four days waiting on a spare part over 500 euros, because the terminal manager's email approval sits in an inbox. I can't point to a specific error rate for anything else, so I'd rather not guess at rework numbers. The proof-of-delivery app has actually been good, though, since I don't get night calls about missing signatures any more.

exchanges.interviewer: Good to hear the proof-of-delivery app solved that. On the forklift delays, can you recall a specific recent time this happened - how long that particular forklift was down and what it held up?
exchanges.reply: I don't have the exact log for a specific forklift in front of me, so I can't give you the precise date or the exact downtime with confidence. What I can say is that the pattern is familiar: a machine goes down, the part is over 500 euros so it needs the terminal manager's email approval, and it waits three or four days while that sits in an inbox. The usual knock-on is that loading slows on that side of the dock and the lads have to work round the machine, but for the exact case and what it held up, the maintenance records or the terminal manager would have the detail.

exchanges.interviewer: Understood, no exact log to hand. Beyond the handover form and the forklift approvals, is there any other recurring problem - even a smaller one - that slows the shift down or causes frustration?
exchanges.reply: Not really, nothing else that I'd call a regular problem. The walk-the-floor recheck after a lost handover form is the other one that keeps coming back, but that's already covered. The rest of the shift mostly runs fine with the team I've got.

exchanges.interviewer: Is there anything important about your work that I didn't ask about?
exchanges.reply: Not really, I think we've covered the main things. The only thing I'd add is that most of the shift runs well, and the team is the reason for that, so if you talk to any of the lads on my rota they'll tell you the same. The handover paper and the forklift approvals are the two things I'd really want fixed, and the proof-of-delivery app has been a genuine improvement.

Hi, thanks for taking the time. To start, could you tell me about your role as morning shift supervisor and who you mainly work with day to day?

exchanges.interviewer: Kiitos, tämä auttaa hahmottamaan tilannetta. Mitkä ovat sinun päävastuusi vuoron aikana - esimerkiksi henkilöstön ohjaus, laiturien aikataulutus vai jotain muuta?
exchanges.reply: Päivän alussa luen yön vuoropaperin, ja sen perusteella selvitän, mitä jäi kesken. Laiturien aikataulutus hoituu meillä taululla, ja se toimii hyvin nykyisellä volyymilla. Aamulla dispatch soittaa ja kysyy, mitä yöstä jäi auki, joten vastaan siihen samalla kun ohjaan lastaus- ja purkutyötä.

exchanges.interviewer: Voitko kertoa tarkemmin siitä yövuoroparista - mitä tietoja siinä tyypillisesti on, ja mistä tunnistat, mitä jäi kesken?
exchanges.reply: Vuoropaperiin yövuoro kirjaa yleensä vaurioituneet lavat, keskeneräiset lähetykset ja ne kuormat, jotka eivät ehtineet lähtemään. Kesken jääneet asiat tunnistan siitä, mitä paperiin on merkitty, mutta käsiala on usein niin huonoa, että joudun arvaamaan. Kun paperi puuttuu kokonaan, kävelen koko terminaalin läpi etsimään vaurioituneita lavoja ja avoimia lähetyksiä, ja sellaiseen menee helposti puoli tuntia, joka on useita kertoja viikossa.

exchanges.interviewer: Tuo on merkittävä löydös - käsialan tulkinta ja paperin puuttuminen vie aikaa useita kertoja viikossa. Palataan vielä siihen myöhemmin. Kun dispatch soittaa aamulla, mitä tietoja te tarkalleen vaihdatte puhelussa?
exchanges.reply: Dispatch kysyy, mitä yöstä jäi keskeneräiseksi, eli mitkä kuormat eivät lähteneet ja mitkä lähetykset ovat vielä kesken. Koska he eivät näe paperilomaketta, minun pitää lukea vastaukset suoraan siitä, ja jos käsiala on epäselvä, puhelu venyy ja joudun varmistamaan asioita. Käytännössä puhelu on siis se kanava, jolla dispatch saa tiedon yöstä.

exchanges.interviewer: Kerro viimeisimmästä kerrasta, kun puhelu venyi epäselvän käsialan takia - kauanko puhelu tavallisesti kestää, ja kuinka paljon pidempi se oli silloin?
exchanges.reply: En ole kirjannut puhelujen kestoa ylös, joten en osaa antaa tarkkaa lukua. Tavallinen puhelu on minulta lyhyt, muutama minuutti, mutta kun käsiala on huono, joudun välillä katsomaan rivin uudelleen ja varmistamaan kuorman numeron, ja silloin puhelu venyy helposti useita minuutteja pidemmäksi.

exchanges.interviewer: Entä mitä tapahtuu puhelun jälkeen - kuka käyttää dispatchille kertomiasi tietoja seuraavaksi, esimerkiksi reittisuunnittelussa tai asiakasviestinnässä?
exchanges.reply: En tiedä tarkalleen, mitä dispatch tekee tiedoilla puhelun jälkeen, koska se ei kuulu minun työhöni. Tiedän vain, että he tarvitsevat sen, jotta tietävät mitkä kuormat lähtevät ja mitkä jäävät odottamaan.

exchanges.interviewer: Selvä, se riittää tähän. Onko muita vastaanottajia yövuoron tiedoille dispatchin lisäksi, esimerkiksi asiakaspalvelu tai varastonhallinta?
exchanges.reply: En osaa sanoa varmasti, kuka muu yövuoron tiedoista hyötyy, koska en ole itse seurannut sitä. Omasta näkökulmastani tieto kulkee yöstä aamuun paperilla ja sitten dispatchille puhelimessa, eikä minulla ole tietoa siitä, välittyykö se edelleen asiakaspalveluun tai varastonhallintaan.

exchanges.interviewer: Mitä paperille tapahtuu sen jälkeen, kun olet lukenut sen ja puhelu dispatchin kanssa on käyty - arkistoitko sen, vai heitetäänkö se pois?
exchanges.reply: Paperi jää yleensä terminaalin toimistoon, ja sen säilytyksestä ja arkistoinnista huolehtii yleensä joku muu, minulla ei ole siitä tarkkaa tietoa. En ole itse ryhtynyt arkistoimaan sitä mihinkään erikseen, joten en osaa sanoa, kuinka kauan se säilyy tai mitä siitä tehdään myöhemmin.

exchanges.interviewer: Kun käsiala on epäselvä, miten yleensä toimit - arvaatko parhaan tulkinnan, vai käytkö tarkistamassa jotain muuta kautta ennen kuin kerrot dispatchille?
exchanges.reply: Yleensä arvaan ensin parhaan tulkinnan kontekstin perusteella, esimerkiksi kuorman numeron ja reitin mukaan. Jos en ole varma, käyn katsomassa lavat tai lähetykset itse lastauslaiturilla, ja silloin ajan kulumista on taas vaikea arvioida tarkasti.

exchanges.interviewer: Oletko koskaan antanut dispatchille väärän tiedon arvauksen perusteella, joka sitten huomattiin vääräksi myöhemmin?
exchanges.reply: En muista yhtään tapausta, jossa olisin antanut dispatchille väärän tiedon ja se olisi huomattu vasta myöhemmin. Koska arvaan vain silloin, kun en pysty tarkistamaan, pyrin kuitenkin käymään lavat tai lähetykset itse läpi ennen kuin kerron. En ole kuitenkaan kirjannut tällaisia tilanteita ylös, joten en osaa sanoa varmasti, eikä minulla ole tietoa siitä, huomaako kukaan virheitä jälkikäteen.

exchanges.interviewer: That's helpful context - no known downstream errors, just the physical check as a safeguard. Besides the handwriting issue, are there other kinds of problems or mistakes that come up regularly during your shift?
exchanges.reply: Käsialan lisäksi tärkein ongelma on se, että paperi puuttuu joskus kokonaan, ja silloin joudun kävelemään terminaalin läpi etsimään vaurioituneita lavoja ja avoimia lähetyksiä. Muuten päivät sujuvat yleensä hyvin, ja laiturien aikataulutus taululla toimii meille hyvin nykyisellä määrällä.

exchanges.interviewer: How often does the paper go missing entirely - is that a daily thing, or more like once or twice a week?

exchanges.interviewer: Kiitos tarkennuksesta - pari minuuttia käsialaongelmaan sopii hyvin kuvaan. Kun lähdet kävelemään terminaalia läpi puuttuvan paperin takia, keskeytyykö samalla muu työsi, kuten laitureiden ohjaus?
exchanges.reply: Kyllä, kun lähden kävelemään terminaalin läpi, joudun jättämään laiturien ohjauksen hetkeksi, ja muut ryhmän jäsenet jatkavat lastausta ilman minua. Yleensä siitä ei tule suurta ongelmaa, mutta kun kävely venyy, kysymykset jäävät odottamaan, kunnes palaan takaisin.

Hi, thanks for taking the time. To start, can you tell me a bit about your role as a transport planner — what you're mainly responsible for day to day?
exchanges.reply: Sure, thanks for having me. My main job is planning the routes for our trucks, so on a normal day I'm looking after about 45 vehicles across the Vantaa area and further out, making sure every load gets to the right place in the right window. I do all of that in the TMS, the transport management system, and honestly route planning is the part that works really well for me. I can rebuild a route in a few minutes when a customer calls to move a delivery, and I can see straight away which driver is free and which truck has the capacity. Once the trucks are out, I keep an eye on how the day is going and deal with whatever comes up, like a late pickup at the terminal or a customer who wants a different time slot. It's busy, but it's the kind of busy I like.

exchanges.interviewer: That sounds like a role with a lot of moving parts. Besides the TMS, who do you mainly work with day to day — drivers, customers, terminal staff?
exchanges.reply: Mostly drivers and the terminal, honestly, and customers come in when something changes. The drivers are on their phones all day, and since we rolled out the proof-of-delivery app, I get signatures and photos in the TMS within minutes of each drop, which has cut disputes about deliveries to almost nothing. The terminal is where the trucks are loaded and where the night shift leaves things, so I'm talking to them constantly about what's ready and what's late. Finance is in the loop too, though more at the end of the day, when I send the delivery details over for billing. Fuel cards and maintenance go through the fleet manager, and those just work, so I don't spend much time on them.

exchanges.interviewer: You mentioned sending delivery details to finance for billing at the end of the day — can you walk me through what that process looks like, step by step?
exchanges.reply: So after the deliveries are done, I go into the TMS and pull up each completed shipment, and for every one I copy the shipment number, the weight, and any extra charges like waiting time into the billing spreadsheet that finance uses. Then I check the rows against what the TMS shows, because one wrong digit means a wrong invoice and somebody in finance has to chase it. It takes me about 90 minutes every afternoon, and honestly that's the part of my day I dislike most. It's all copying from one screen to another, and I know it's exactly the kind of thing a machine should be doing. I'd happily see that link automated.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a clear case of manual double-handling. How many shipments roughly do you copy over like that each day?
exchanges.reply: Roughly 45 trucks go out a day, and most of them do two or three drops, so I'd estimate somewhere around 100 to 130 shipment lines a day. Some are simple, a single pallet with no extras, but a fair number carry waiting time or a second stop, and those take a bit longer to get right. On a busy day I can feel how tired my eyes get by the end of the 90 minutes. I don't have an exact count in front of me, though, because the number changes so much with the season and the customer mix. If finance wants the precise figure, the TMS export or the billing sheet itself would give you the real number.

exchanges.interviewer: That gives a good sense of scale. Walking through a concrete recent one — what format is the billing spreadsheet, is it Excel, shared online, something else?
exchanges.reply: I'm honestly not sure of the exact format, to be fair. As far as I know it's a spreadsheet that finance keeps, and I add my rows to it, but whether it's an Excel file on a shared drive or something hosted online is a question for finance. What I can tell you is what I see on my side: I have the TMS open in one window and the billing sheet in another, and I type across by hand. If you want the specifics, someone in finance would know exactly how it's stored and who has access.

exchanges.interviewer: That's fair, finance would know the technical side. Does the TMS let you export those shipment details at all, or is manual copy-paste the only way to get data out?
exchanges.reply: I'm not certain what the TMS export options are, to be honest. I've never had to use an export, because I've always just worked from the screen and typed across. I'd guess there's some kind of report or download function since most systems have one, but I don't know whether it gives you the fields finance needs in the layout they use. The fleet manager or whoever administers the TMS would be the one to ask. If there is an export, it could be worth looking at before anyone builds a bigger fix.

exchanges.interviewer: Good to know — that's worth flagging for whoever looks into this. Thinking about yesterday specifically, roughly how many of those 100-130 lines did you have to double-check or fix because something didn't match?
exchanges.reply: I can't give you a precise number for yesterday, and I'd rather not make one up. What I can say is that I do check each row against the TMS before I send it, because a single wrong digit in the weight or a missed waiting-time charge turns into a wrong invoice that finance has to chase. Most rows match straight away, but I wouldn't want to guess how many needed a second look on one particular day. If you want an accurate figure, the easiest source would be the corrections or invoice queries that came back from finance, since those would show where the mismatches actually ended up.

exchanges.interviewer: That makes sense, thanks for being upfront about that. Since you've never had reason to try an export, would it be fair to say the TMS administrator or fleet manager is the right person to confirm what export options exist?
exchanges.reply: The TMS administrator is the right person for the technical question, and I'd include the fleet manager too, since they use the system a lot and would know what reports they pull. I'm not sure whether the fleet manager actually administers the TMS, or whether that's someone in IT or the office. Either way, I'd point them to what I described: the shipment number, weight and extra charges that I copy every afternoon. If they can tell you whether those fields come out in a file, that would answer most of the question.

exchanges.interviewer: Good, that's clear. Switching gears a bit — what does your screen actually look like in the TMS when you're planning routes, is it a map view, a list of jobs, something else?
exchanges.reply: It's a mix, and I like that about it. The main planning view is a list of jobs on the left, each with its pickup, drop, time window and weight, and when I drag a job onto a truck the route updates on a map on the right. So I can see the stops and the travel times at a glance, and I can tell straight away if a truck is over capacity or would miss a delivery window. I can also see which drivers are available and which vehicles are free, all in the same screen, which saves me a lot of phoning around. I don't use the map as much as the list, honestly, because the list is faster when I'm moving ten jobs at once. I couldn't tell you the exact layout settings, though, since I just use what's been set up for us.

exchanges.interviewer: When a job comes in to move a delivery, like that customer call you mentioned earlier — do you make the change directly in that list view, or is there another step first?
exchanges.reply: Usually I do it directly in the list view. If the new slot clashes with another delivery, the TMS flags it, and I shuffle one of the other jobs before I confirm. The only extra step is when the customer wants a change that affects a driver who's already on the road, because then I have to phone the driver, since the app doesn't push route changes as far as I know. Most calls are sorted in a couple of minutes this way.

exchanges.interviewer: That's a useful detail about the driver app not pushing live updates. When you have to phone a driver mid-route about a change, how does that update eventually get back into the TMS?

exchanges.interviewer: Good to hear the POD app works that well. Outside of billing mismatches, is there another spot — maybe route conflicts or driver comms — where things commonly go wrong or cause rework?

exchanges.interviewer: That paper handover sounds like a daily friction point. Can you walk me through a recent morning — what's on that paper, and what do you typically end up phoning about?
